While I am dealing with the question of phosphates, Mr. Speaker, might I be permitted to answer a question by the hon. member for Kootenay West, asked on October 30, in regard to the International Joint Commission report. The report referred to by the hon. member was submitted to the International Joint Commission by the advisory boards established by the commission to investigate and report on water pollution in Lakes Erie and Ontario and the international reach of the St. Lawrence River downstream from Lake Ontario.

In the present speech she was restored as though she were some person from some foreign land who has shown some interest in Canada. I repeat, there shall be one Parliament consisting of the Queen and Upper House, styled the Senate, and the House of Commons, with an executive government with authority of and over Canada declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.

I may not be as amusing or interesting as the previous speaker, but I shall try to be more serious.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), as well as the leaders of the other parties and the hon. members who have spoken during this debate have done so with great dignity and generally without any bias. They made a general survey of the political situation inside and outside Canada.
I noticed that there was general agreement as to the alarming situation brought about by such problems as inflation, price increases, the cost of living, international insecurity, starvation in the world and the impatience of the young in face of our inability to solve their problems quickly.

Finally, I have noticed a general consensus to the effect that we should all work together very hard to seek and find solutions.
In the Speech from the Throne, the government proposes to call upon the House to study various papers, as well as legislative proposals intended to lower the voting age to 18, devise measures to fight pollution and general inflation, and reform social security to build a strong and productive country.
The Prime Minister, in the course of this debate, has referred, among other things, to Canada's human and material resources, constructive criticism on the part of the opposition, the needless pollution of air and water, the participation of the young people in our country's political life, inflation, the increase in the cost of living, the inequality of opportunities for well-being in the world, threats to the human race in general, the Arctic regions, Canada's sovereignty and many other subjects.
During the debates which will take place in this House about the bills or problems that will be considered, I hope that I shall have the opportunity to take the floor as often as possible. However, in case I could not do so in due course, I take this opportunity today to give my impressions about a few points in which I am particularly interested, namely the very serious situation prevailing at present in the Middle East, the recognition of the People's Republic of China in opposition to Nationalist China, the problem of prisoners' rehabilitation and of expunging criminal records and finally, of bail in general.
In the Middle East, Mr. Speaker, we all know that peace has practically never prevailed there since the end of the ice-age,

The area of compensation arrangements for members of parliament is a delicate one. It is time we told the Canadian public what the situation is. I think the professional paper prepared by Mr. Horst G. Wolff, published by the Canadian Tax Foundation and circulated to many, if not all, members is a very useful contribution to this whole question with respect to expenses and compensation arrangements for members of parliament. It is very useful in helping us present the case to the Canadian public. It traces the history and points out the inconsistencies and the lack of a single guiding principle. It attempts to distinguish between the confusions of salaries and expenses and traces how these came about. It points out that the Carter Commission recommended changes and it supports the principle the Carter Commission endorses. One of the recommendations reads:
Members of Parliament should be treated on the same basis as other employees and so should be required to bring their allowances into income, and at the same time should be allowed to deduct their expenses of earning employment income including election expenses. We would expect that it would be accepted that the regular place of business of a Member of Parliament is in his riding, so that all expenses incurred while in Ottawa and in travelling to and from Ottawa would be deductible as long as they fell within the limits established for such expenses.

In other words, the Carter Commission proposal recognizes the dislocations which are occasioned by having two bases-a constituency base and an Ottawa base. This article points out clearly that the prevailing practice in business and the professions is for businessmen to deduct out-of-pocket expenses incurred away from their place of business. For instance, if a businessman or, indeed, anyone else, were to come to Ottawa to appear before one of our committees his expenses in coming to Ottawa would be deductible; they would not be added to his income as they are by inference to ours.

An appropriate way to do so would be by establishing a commission which would be given the task of determining what should be the appropriate level of remuneration for Members of Parliament by comparing the levels applicable in industry, the professions and the public service. More particularly, it is important that such a commission should recommend a way of providing for future changes in the salaries of parliamentarians. The present system was designed for parttime members. It is an ad hoc arrangement and in my view it is no longer appropriate since it no longer serves the cause which it espouses, that is to say, the health of parliamentary democracy.
Let there be no mistake about this: Members of parliament will be asked to do more, not less; legislation will become more complicated and more technical, and the effectiveness of members of parliament will become increasingly important to the operation of this system, not less. To point a finger at an example which may be useful in this context, I should like to remind hon. members that some time ago the United States recognized the importance of setting up a public commission to determine the appropriate levels and methods of compensating their members of parliament. I refer to the Kettle Commission which reported not long ago.
I think the commission should include members who are well-known in business life, in labour organizations and perhaps in one of the professions. I am thinking of a university president. Unless the system of public service is changed, good men will not serve in parliament in the future, not because they are unprepared to do so but because parliament and the people are not prepared to face a basic issue. Formation of such a commission as I have proposed would be an important step in the process of parliamentary reform, of bringing this institution up to date; of preserving the role of parliament in an increasingly complex age; of ensuring respect for this institution and for the quality of its representation; in short, of developing a strong and healthy parliamentary democracy in Canada.

I should like then to take advantage of the few minutes at my disposal to outline briefly what I consider the essential problems at the present time.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
How far will the ever growing anarchy go? When will it stop?
Parents no longer know whether their children are in school or on the streets, whether they prepared a Molotov cocktail at lunch time, blew up the school buildings, picketed, marched or maybe even had a study session. In fact, those are the actions of professional agitators who, as the Quebec premier said recently, are interested in emptying our schools for any reason they can find, in making our children, inspired by deceitful and hate propaganda, come down into the street.
Right-minded people who favour order, authority and justice must and will have to get a consensus to end the underhand doings of some bearded and immigrant activists who left their country for fear of not being free and respected and who now want to impose their opinions in our country, without respecting anything, or anybody and foster anarchy. Those people wish to create here what they left behind when they fled their country. This points to a deficiency in the government's immigration policy.
The mother does not know any longer whether her husband will work tomorrow or if he will not return in the evening and tell her: "I am on strike."
The sick do not know any longer whether they will get the necessary basic care to which they are strictly entitled to recover at least part of their health.
Teachers do not know any longer whether they will be paid or if they will be provided with some kind of teaching material.

DEBATES	November 4, 1969
Students cannot tell whether they will attend school tomorrow.
Mr. Speaker, we must not close our eyes to the fact that in our schools and universities, drugs and narcotics are flowing freely, and authority is being thrown overboard. Unfortunately, I find that few of my colleagues are interested in those questions.
The young unemployed despair of ever finding jobs in which they can make use of the skills they have acquired.
Wheat producers accumulate surpluses but they do not know what to do with them.
Milk producers in the East must pour their milk down the drain this year-I deeply regret that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is not in the house-not knowing what to do with their product when two thirds of the world's population are starving to death and are without the bare minimum. While people are starving to death, while some families do not have the bare necessaries, we are wasting our production.
Mr. Speaker, our rural community is becoming urbanized and this results in complete disruption. We are not prepared, nor are our governments, to cope with such changes.
All have questions to ask. However, few answers arouse interest.
As far as the Throne Speech is concerned, it is a vacuum. As a matter of fact, all those problems I have just listed-and I have only mentioned a few-have the same common denominator: social injustice.
The just society was not supposed to materialize yesterday and, according to the Speech from the Throne, it will not be for tomorrow either.
Personally, I had been building several hopes on the Throne Speech of this second session, Mr. Speaker, I bitterly realize, as many others, you may believe me, that nothing will be done this year except for rehashing the old bills and old ideas of the first session which brought no economical improvement for that matter.
Social injustice, that is what we must fight against. However, to fight it, we must first expose it, see it, grasp it. And to grasp it, we must go to its roots. We must go back to the source of economic injustices. That is the fundamental point I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and a great number of other intellectuals of the same school speak forcefully of the just society and social justice which we must establish
November 4, 1969

and in older to achieve that aim, the Prime Minister has developed a program which may be summarized as follows: to appoint task forces, to produce white papers, to organize study trips across Canada, to submit reports and more reports which will he on shelves, to put the axe in the public service, to modernize the Criminal Code and give much importance to secondary bills such as those on abortion, homosexuality, etc., to impose credit restrictions to everyone except the rich, to increase interest rates on ah loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, etc., to review all programs without ever changing them, and to tighten one's belt, because inflation is galloping, and it is necessary to save money.
So that is the program of the Prime Minister, since he became leader of the government. Those are the only solutions he has to offer.
In other words, we must deprive ourselves in the hope that poverty will dissappear, and that social disparities will become mathematical equations.
The government also tells us with much publicity: Buy Canada Savings Bonds, they are gold! But with what money? That is what the Prime Minister fails to say.
This amounts to deluding a whole population that wants order, justice, equality and efficiency.
This world, full of inequities caused by the inertia of governments which find satisfaction only in indifference and in provoking futile disputes between governments over red carpets or words, is the best breeding ground for protests, revolutions, violence and anarchy.
Mr. Speaker, it is urgent to tackle the real problems, because it is well known that every social inequality is very often the result of an economic inequality or inequity and that every economic inequality is very often caused by the want of balance between the forces of production and the forces of consumption. So long as there is not a more equitable distribution of products while political freedom is respected, protests will continue to grow and to submerge our country and Quebec.
It seems to me that a certain kind of protest is a rising tide which cannot be stemmed at present, carrying all before it, drowning those who are unwilling to follow the wave of violence unleashed by union leaders such as Michel Chartrand, Raymond Laliberte, Marcel Pepin and others.
The Address-Mr. Fortin
That is why many people today have lost control of the situation and are at wits' end. Moreover, unless we face up to our responsibilities right now and our governments take concrete and immediate action, we will lose not merely our wits, but also our private enterprise, our liberty and our lives.
Tighten your belts. We will send the army in. We will take this or that community under our wings. If that is not enough we will impose price and salary controls. Such are the new proposals put forward by the Prime Minister in this session.
These are like band-aids on a wooden leg, they only aggravate discontent and everything will have to be done over again tomorrow. Why? Because we did not tackle and we are not tackling the real issue, which is a monetary problem. Time has come to act by taking concrete measures.
Mr. Speaker, here is one of many typical examples which really disappointed me last year. It will be recalled that, with great fanfare, the former Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) toured Canada with experts, held hearings with various groups and finally concluded that some measures were needed to solve, at least in part, the housing crisis in Canada.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The report has not only been differed indefinitely but the minister himself was forced to resign in the face of the inaction of the government of which he had been a candidate to the leadership.
This is an example among many which shows that we have now to bear with a government of retarded students who compile notes and decline action, and true commitment. In fact, what we need is a government of action.
Mr. Speaker, in closing I should like to deal with problems such as tight money, unemployment, and interest rates.
In view of the tight money and unemployment situation which we are going through at this time, several unbelievers of the past recognize today the urgent need for a monetary reform. With the Ralliement Creditiste, they agree that unemployment results obviously in economic stagnation. They agree that the great number of bankruptcies in Canada is due more to the tight money policy than to mismanagement.
Everyone realizes also the unfairness of the income tax which robs people, tortures with a shocking off-handedness the morale of those
492	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fortin who built this country and who contribute to the development of our natural resources.
We also witness the impotence of the governments before those who control money and credit. Therefore it is important to delegate to our parliaments, representatives who have a greater concern for their electors than for the political party financed by electoral funds and high finance.
At the present time we are living in a deceitful economy. The prevailing economic conditions are unmerciful and cruel and, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), coming events will prove it.
In fact, if we look closely at the living conditions of many of us, we must admit without any reservation, that our system of government, supposedly democratic and alive, is really pitiful. An untold number of unemployed people and their families are living in poverty in the midst of affluence. Crimes, break-ins, are committed every day by young people who seem to have no place any more in our society.
Those same young people our federal leaders used to feed, to clothe, to care for and to pay all through the war years, they can no longer house them, clothe them, feed them, nor pay them in time of peace nor can they give then a job.
It is to those young people that they used to sing, with a quaver in the voice, the blessings of a war that would restore the human being to its democratic rights.
It is those same young people that our federal leaders are shamefully betraying today, after promising them during the war years an honest and happy in this rich country of ours. Our politicians cannot do anything now for those young people they deliberately sacrifice to finance and the chartered banks.
There is only room now for the dollar sign of finance in the heart of the federal government.
Must our Canadian youth be satisfied with decent living only when it must kill, and should it be starving to death afterwards with the return of peace?
Mr. Speaker, that is the serious question we are asking ourselves. It is all very well to shout that unemployment is international, that inflation preys on democracies, that money is too expensive and that the inkwells of the bankers are empty; it still remains that money is scarce. There are too many products of all kinds in our country. We must tolerate
fMr. Fortin.]
DEBATES	November 4, 1969
destitution within affluence. We must tolerate the fact that the rich grow richer and that the poor get poorer.
Thus, our governments, whether red or blue, restrain production. Factories are closed, good fathers of families are thrown out of work and our youth into a chasm of alarming uncertainty, when it is not into despair.
We suffer from economic anaemia, precisely because the blood that is necessary to the economic body, that is money, becomes increasingly rare through the fault of those who control it: bankers and high finance.
The federal authorities, Mr. Speaker, tolerate and allow the existence through legislative measures, of this anti-human and anti-social system which consists in the sad exploitation of the people, under the sympathetic eye of the present government. "Tighten your belts." That is all we hear.
Mr. Speaker, we need an active government and that may explain the move of protest. In fact, the governments are not moving. We owe it to ourselves to raise against this system which is rotten to the core. It is not brains that are lacking in the head of our people. Nor is it the heart that is lacking in the breast of Canadians, but rather money in their pocket-book, money which opens the doors to affluence in the country. Will not two wars and three economic recessions within 35 years be enough to open our eyes to the bad effects of a perverted finance that enslaves man. Money has always been lavishly spent on war, but it is hard to muster in the cause of peace. Bankers will readily extend their help in time of affluence but if we do happen to need them, then they put the lid back on their bottle of red ink. The tight money policy recently announced in the Speech from the Throne as a mean of fighting inflation gives us the measure of government enslavement to big business which provides the financing for the party's electoral fund.
Bankers, in Canada, are allowed to lay down the law in the economic field and our government has to fall in step, behind them, regardless of its responsibilities. It will lend you an umbrella when the sun is shining but come the first drops of rain and you are left in the street under the downpour. When a federal government, whether grit or tory, thus allows individuals to corner all the wealth of a country like ours without providing for a distribution system which makes allowance for everyone's freedom and safety through a national dividend and compensated discount, such a government deserves to be
November 4, 1969	COMMONS
overthrown or openly questioned. The people themselves are bound to ask such questions.
If we want to put an end to the crisis conditions we are now experiencing, not only in Quebec but also in the other provinces- for the uneasiness now felt by the Quebecers also deeply affects every Canadian in every province-we have to take some kind of action.
Recently, I had the pleasure of going to Nova Scotia. Early in the spring, I had the pleasure of going out west. On those two occasions I was able to see that what Quebecers feel is felt in another language as deeply and with as much concern by the other Canadians.
All are now aware that we must tackle the water pollution problem, the lack of Canadian unity-which was the object of the bill on the official languages,-that the Criminal Code must be amended.
Canadians are pleased with the proposed legislation generally, while recognizing more and more that the problem does not lie there, that we delude ourselves in thinking that the problem exists at that level. The problem goes beyond that. It is a monetary problem and the time has come for us to come to grips with it.
Credit in Canada is the monopoly of the commercial banks despite what some of our colleagues may say. That monopoly was granted by the Bank Act of 1935. The right hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King said so himself in 1935-I am not putting those words in his mouth, as I was not even born at that time. I quote:
Once a country has given up control of its money and its credit, it matters little who makes the laws of the land. Usury, once in command, will lead any country to ruin.
Mackenzie King, that great Liberal leader, said in addition, and I quote:
Until such time as control over the issue of money and credit is given back to the government and recognized as its most obvious, most sacred responsibility, speaking of the sovereignty of parliament is nothing but idle talk.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In the same connection, I feel, to use the words of Mr. Mackenzie King, that it is unnecessary and useless to talk about the sovereignty and independence of Quebec as long as we do not have the tools needed to keep that independence under control
The same remarks could apply to Canada. This is why, in this as in anything else, we
DEBATES	493
The Address-Mr. Fortin are deluding ourselves when we believe in those glib talkers who actually have no economic solution to offer.
Our present monetary system has most disastrous effects. Successive periods of sudden boom and sudden recession keep recurring much too frequently.
The cycle, due moreover to the action of the financial system supported by our country at the present time,, is the following:
When peace supersedes war, surplus production accumulates and reveals the lack of purchasing power of the people. The shortage of outlets for our products brings about two results: first of all, unemployment, which, in turn, causes economic crises, and then follow the clashes that prompt some countries to wage war, and war, inevitably, involves increased borrowing, debt and inflation. To cope with the situation, governments, under the present system of administration, claim that they must increase taxes in all fields. Such levies snowball.
Then peace returns and the cycle referred to starts over again. On reading Canada's history, as well as that of many other countries, one can see that this is true.
Considering the fact that the control of the issue and withdrawal of money may determine the value and the nature of the production, it is when our fellow-citizens can exercise their sovereign right to control the monetary system through their parliament that the individual can be assured of financial security and freedom of action in the economic field.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I condemn the emptiness of the Speech from the Throne which does not offer any solution to the present problems, but only encourages people to become entangled in the system, thereby increasing their displeasure. I find it most unfortunate that instead of tackling the real problem, the real opponents of financial progress, we are satisfied, with the government's consent and under its impulse, to waste our time with secondary legislation while the financial problems only grow worse.
Mr. Speaker, I find unthinkable that the people should be so poorly informed. If they really knew something about the present economic system, instead of wasting their time protesting about a lot of secondary things, they would do so about the real problem which is a monetary one.
What is perhaps most unfortunate is that the Speech from the Throne does not recommend any action to solve the problem. Maybe

The Address-Mr. Rochon
it is an indication that this government is in no way different from the previous ones.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like those who spoke before me, I would like first of all to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
During the last session, my colleague from Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) expressed some of his opinions but through the style and the assurance he displayed last week, he showed us in a subtle and entirely new way that we were right last year to foresee a brilliant and promising future for him. Having heard his speech, I am sure as are all my colleagues that his contribution to Canadian politics will do credit not only to his province but also to the whole country.
As for the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), he admitted that we were right when we were saying to his predecessor, Mr. Gregoire, that his separatist ideas were not shared by most of his constituents, but very few of them. Indeed, when he advocated that isolationist doctrine, he was forgetting that the federal and provincial governments had contributed the most to the development of that Quebec area known today throughout the world as the aluminum country.
Our colleague admitted that we were right when he stated his views and those of the people who voted for him at the last election. He made us understand, as we had told Mr. Gregoire, that in the riding of Lapointe as elsewhere in Quebec, people realize that Quebec cannot live and develop without the remainder of Canada and moreover, the remainder of the country needs Quebec to assert itself as a country whose advice is sought and followed.
Furthermore, I wish to congratulate our leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and to thank him for putting his intelligence at the service of the nation. Whatever you hear, he has become for us the members of his party, a source of inspiration, a guiding light in our action. God knows that the need for action is all too frequent in this century when what is essential today is already outdated tomorrow, in this century of the atom and of electronics when too often, alas, the machine takes the place of man, in this century when we have seen astronauts walking on the moon's surface.
Mr. Speaker, as my time is rather short, may I deal immediately with the subject of which I wish to speak and to express my views on some of today's problems.

I do not intend to pay attention to the criticism voiced by the members of the opposition. I know they did so without malice or spite, but rather to help the government. At least, it should be so.
I know that we, in this house, cannot all think the same way, but I know that all of us share the same ambition: to try and improve the welfare of the people. The only difference between us is in the way we see things. One wants to put one's own ideas forward and, without being fully aware of it, one slides towards partisanship, which is perfectly human. One unwillingly impedes the smooth running of the nation's business, instead of joining with others and helping others. One goes sometimes as far as to question the good faith of some who, more than opponents, would like to co-operate.
Everything should not be accepted straight away, for the government could make mistakes, errors and even blunders.
Moreover the opposition's function is to keep an eye on the government. If one were prepared to make constructive suggestions instead of blaming and criticizing, as is too often the case, the whole population would benefit and everyone would be happy to be efficient and understanding.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
For a few years, Mr. Speaker, the throne speeches have been dealing mainly with federal-provincial relations with a view to assuring the welfare of each citizen in every province. The numerous pieces of legislation passed, both economic and social, stand as a clear evidence that federal authorities are always eager to co-operate in the best interests of the Canadian people, and that, in order to attain that goal, confederation has to be oriented in a very specific direction for us to become a big nation in a big country.
This year again, the same end is in view, but times have changed. In 1969, it has become difficult and extremely hazardous to tackle the problems in the same manner as before. We must have the courage to face facts and to bring forward up-dated solutions, because let us not forget that we have to take into account, on the one hand, the new needs of a large number of countries in full development, in the process of great economic expansion and, on the other hand, the rights of the provinces. Even with the best of intentions, one may appear to be meddling in fields where this would jeopardize autonomy and lead to conflict between authorities of which, sad to say, those who are steeped in a narrow
November 4, 1969

and retrograde brand of nationalism take advantage to further a cause which has no justification in this century of emancipation in which we achieved maturity.
Last year, the main theme of the Speech from the Throne was the "just society". This year, the objective is to prepare the future by increasing the efficiency of present programs. What is announced is not the launching of major ventures, but rather the continuation of the fight against inflation. However, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which, as all are aware, has been created to do away with social disparities, will intensify its activity.
Numerous projects have been announced in the speech. Previous speakers have submitted a few to the House, in the public interest or in that of their riding. Some suggested that the unemployment insurance program be thoroughly revamped, others advocated certain changes in housing policies, others still showed us the advantages of certain reforms concerning the rights of the individual, with a concern for more respect for man, his person and what he represents. All these comments and analyses clearly demonstrated that the government is prepared to act, especially on domestic issues. This was pointed out in an article published in Montreal's La Presse, and I quote:
Domestic issues are given precedence in the Speech from the Throne. Indeed, the few paragraphs devoted to foreign affairs merely recall a well known policy: the government's intention to participate in the establishment of a movement designed to bring about a reform of the U.N., increased assistance to developing countries, and the initiative from Ottawa to protect international waters from pollution.
And that newspaperman went on to say:
Whether it is a matter of tax reform, of the revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act, or of different suggestions concerning consumer credit, packaging, identification of textile products and the security of motor vehicles, as well as of amendments to the Criminal Code, these different pieces of legislation tend to increase the security of the individual in the face of the growing power of the state and the complexity of the industrial society.
Even in the economic field, the government gives high priority to its concern for the welfare of the individual; the paragraph of the speech devoted to housing, in which the government announces as an objective the building of one million housing units and homes in five years is designed to lessen the difficulties of the less affluent.
Also designed for the individual are the following measures: the implementation of the official language bill, the fight against pollution, assistance for depressed areas, and lower income groups, the

The Address-Mr. Rochon
reform of social security, and also, the tax reform which aims at a more equitable distribution of the tax burden while favouring the economic expansion in the country.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, these few remarks about the Speech from the Throne, let me borrow this sentence from the Prime Minister. I quote:
All these measures tend to develop the environment where Canadians work and live. Even if such an environment became idyllic, there still would remain a very important task to perform, a task that will never be completed: guarantee to every citizen a life protected against any undue intervention.
Mr. Speaker, I had the great honour, last June, to represent Canada at the NATO meetings in Brussels. As vice-chairman of the scientific committee, I was asked to submit my appreciation of the studies concerning the marine resources of the North Atlantic area. Those information documents dealt first of all with the deep-sea resources in fish and aquatic vegetation, including sea-weeds, and it said that in a not too distant future perhaps, the ocean would become the granary of the world, and that the culture of these sea-weeds would probably become an important source of raw material for the manufacture food and industrial products.
It said that although these questions have been discussed before by other international agencies, the FAO for example, it could be useful for these NATO countries to promote the study of the techniques that are particularly adapted to the situation in the North Atlantic area, which would allow for increased exchanges of information, so that each of the member countries could benefit from these studies and be in a position to fight with the greatest effectiveness possible against this calamity, which is pollution.
Like other members of the committee, I have been quite impressed with these reports and I have come to the conclusion that means had to be found at all cost to protect all that wealth and to check water pollution.
As mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, our water resources are immense of course but they are not inexhaustible, and if it is imperative to encourage their development, it is just as urgent to ensure their conservation. Lakes, rivers and streams, are befouled with rotting marine vegetation, the sad result quite often of our lack of foresight.
Aware of its responsibilities, the government has made known its views on this serious pollution problem and it has initiated consultations with the provinces. So much the
November 4, 1969

The Address-Mr. Rochon better, and I shall make it my duty to send to Colonel Driscoll, the same gentleman who in October 1968 published in Foreign Affairs a most informed study on this serious problem, the part which deals with the subject.
During this tour, I had the opportunity to hear several guest speakers deal with the ticklish problem of pollution, at various NATO meetings. And one of the reports which impressed me most is, without doubt, the preliminary report on the United States reaction to the oil pollution off Santa Barbara, submitted by Mr. Peter Rondino, vicepresident and reporting officer of the International Secretariat.
I shall not go into all the details of that report. I think it suffices to say that on Tuesday, January 28, 1969, an eruption occurred during drilling operations in a well of the Union Oil Company about six miles from Santa Barbara. The well was capped so as to prevent oil from flowing too fast, but oil slicks finally covered the sea and the American government had to step in so as to protect one of the most beautiful beaches in the world. In fact, on April 16, the House of Representatives passed the 1969 Water Quality Improvement Act, for the protection of public waters against oil pollution. The Act contains a provision as to the responsibility inherent to oil plants. While discussing such a provision-I still refer to the Rondino report-the members of the government favoured a concept of absolute responsibility. Besides, Secretary Hickel has already published regulations to that effect and one of the exploration conditions, under a contract signed with the American government, is that the operators' activities should not be harmful in any way to the environment and, should they be, the said operators would be responsible.	.
Furthermore, the American Senate is now trying to determine whether full responsibility for cleaning up, without any kind of limitation, could not be covered by insurance.
This, Mr. Speaker, is perhaps a drastic measure but if you consider the awful damage incurred, on the one hand, and public interest on the other, there can be no hesitation. Other countries, including ours, should do the same. I was very much interested in another report, that of a Dutch delegate whose name I have forgotten. It dealt with air pollution resulting from the chimney fumes from factories located on the shores of the North Sea, on the outskirts of the city

of Amsterdam. Contact with the outside air changed these fumes into toxic gas and the resulting fall-out in the sea water was endangering the very life of the schools of fish living in those waters. The Dutch government, under the provisions of a bill passed by the legislative assembly, then compelled the owners of those plants, as well as any person potentially responsible for such mishaps, to use the necessary equipment in order to counter the danger of pollution.
Why could we not do the same thing?
Everywhere in the world, Mr. Speaker, people are rightly alarmed by this national threat. I am sure the government, together with the provinces, will find some way of doing something about it. If ever I am fortunate enough to go back to NATO, I would be glad to say that in Canada we also want to make a contribution to the well-being of man in this particular field.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
To all the reasons that could be put forth in favour of adapting a national program for the control of water pollution, another can be added, quite personal perhaps, since north of Montreal where my riding is located a river flows whose waters are so polluted that the Health League in Quebec stated publicly, early last summer, and I quote:
We hereby advise summer visitors, whether they live on the North shore, in Ville Laval, or on the South shore, in Montreal, along the Back River, that bathing is dangerous and that typhoid cases have been attributed to bathing in those waters.
I understand that sums were voted by the government, two years ago, when I was the member for Laval. Indeed, even at that time I asked for the Milles-Iles and Prairies rivers to be dredged and cleaned.
I know that in order to check inflation the government was forced to adopt an austerity program; I also know that, in that frame of mind, that work was postponed. But, might it not be indicated, as a start in the fight against that plague, to forbid bathing in rivers where there is danger of catching typhoid fever?
Since I have mentioned my riding, perhaps I could point out that our post office, on Hen-ri-Bourassa street, is too small. For several years now, we have asked that a new post office be built, capable of serving a population of over half a million people in northern Montreal, from Cremazie street to Riviere des Prairies, and from Ville St. Laurent to Ville Montreal-Nord. I am merely mentioning this urgent need as I will deal again with the
November 4, 1969

question when we consider the estimates of the Post Office Department.
Another question which I would have liked to discuss and which is of great interest to the Quebec members is what is taking place in our province. What is the meaning of all those protests which border on anarchy if not revolution? With the limited time at my disposal I cannot deal with it immediately, but I will surely find an occasion to come back on the subject in the course of this session. I will only say now that a few agitators have deceived too many people. The majority of the people are not separatists, far from it, as they are on the whole proud of being Canadians. These people desire mostly one thing: the fulfilment of the Canadian nation that they love and would like to be esteemed by the world at large

Mr. Speaker, first of all may I join with other hon. members who have participated in this debate in extending the usual perfunctory words of congratulation to the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
May I also, with the indulgence of the House, avail myself of this opportunity to make an apology. When the House met last session to wind up its affairs on October 22, I rose in my place on a question of privilege and inadvertently misled the house by suggesting that the 13th report of the transport committee had omitted a very important part of its recommendations. I subsequently discovered, Mr. Speaker, that there was a 14th report and that this report contained the part that I thought had been omitted. Therefore, I should like to apologize to the House for having inadvertently misled hon. members. May I apologize in particular to the chairman of the transport committee, the hon. member for LaSalle (Mr. Lessard), for having cast his position in some doubt.
I have been listening with great interest to this debate on the address, as I did to the speech itself. I have since read it a number of times to try to find some glimmer of hope that the many problems facing the country, and particularly some of the special and peculiar problems facing the Atlantic area, will be dealt with.
I have also listened to the various ministers who have participated in the debate, and with special interest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson). As a member of the House
The Address-Mr, McGrath representing a Newfoundland constituency, to say that I was disappointed with the content of the minister's speech is to put it mildly. There was the usual fluency and eloquence, the usual sound and fury, but as usual nothing was said.
This was a great disappointment to me because I expected the minister, who sits in the cabinet as a representative of my province, to enunciate some of the solutions to the serious problems facing the Atlantic region. I expected him to outline what the government proposes to do about them and how it proposes to cope with them. But, as I say, I was greatly disappointed, as I am greatly disappointed by the minister's absence from the House today.

Yes, again, as my colleague for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador interjects. We have had to wait for other speeches to inform us whether new light was to be shed upon some of our serious problems. Again, we have been disappointed.
Yesterday the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) made a speech to which we listened with interest and followed closely. We have a great deal of sympathy for the minister; we have a great deal of support for some of the things we believe he is trying to do. The minister referred at great length to conservation and pollution. I should like to deal very briefly with the subject of pollution because it is a problem with which we are all concerned, one which is reaching crisis proportions in this country.
I believe that pollution in its various forms is one of the most serious problems facing Canada, but I should like to deal with but one aspect, an aspect that the minister of fisheries referred to in his speech yesterday, namely the effect of pollution on marine life.
The Government of Canada has recently finally recognized-I hope this recognition has not come too late-the severity of pollution in Canada. The pollution of our marine resources has taken on new aspects, and later on I should like to refer to them. A great deal of attention has been paid to the pollution of our lakes and rivers. Similarly, a great deal of attention has been focussed on the pollution of our major inland waters. I might say I am glad to see the minister, under whose jurisdiction this pollution problem comes, is in his seat. We have all heard a great deal about the disastrous effects that pollution has had on our freshwater fishing industry. In many

disaster a few years ago when this tanker, with a full load of crude oil, broke up on the rocks off the coast of England. It is interesting to note that even though this accident took place several years ago, the oil pollution resulting from it is still a major problem. Scientists are still, to this very day, trying to measure scientifically the disastrous effect this accident had on the marine life of that part of the world. As oil tankers go, the Torrey Canyon was not a large ship. As a matter of fact, by today's standards she could be considered a small ship.
If one were to compare the Torrey Canyon to one of the small supertankers or compare it to the Manhattan, one would find the comparison dramatic. The Manhattan is 106,000 tons with a carrying capacity of 38 million gallons of oil, enough I am told to fill 4,000 railway tank cars. According to an article in the trade magazine Oil Week for September 29, 1969 we can expect ships much larger than the Manhattan to operate in the Northwest Passage. According to this same article-and surely this must be considered as a good authority-we can expect anywhere from 25 to 30 tankers in the next 10 years, tankers of 250,000 tons or more, to be operating in the Northwest Passage. These are tankers capable of carrying in excess of 1.7 million barrels of oil. When one compares this to the capacity of the Torrey Canyon, one can realize the enormity of the pollution threat.
As I said, too little is known about oil pollution on the high seas. Practically nothing, however, is known about oil pollution in the Arctic. From what little scientific data there is available regarding the decomposition of oil waste on the high seas, scientists will agree that decomposition slows markedly as the temperature is lowered. It follows, therefore, that the oil waste dumped on Arctic ice must be preserved, according to the best scientific evidence I can find, from decomposition and hence would represent a continuing pollution threat. Perhaps this is the dawn of the "Silent Spring" unless something is done about it. The sinking or even the serious damaging of but one of these tankers in this area could and would have a serious long term effect on the whole Arctic and Atlantic coastal environment, not only for our marine living resources under the sea but also those over the sea.
According to a paper prepared for the Canadian Wild Life Service by Dr. Richard E. Warner of Memorial University, Canadian resources will bear the brunt of any such

The Address-Mr. McGrath accident. I should like to quote the very important words of Professor Warner, a well known and learned expert in this field.
In the present absence of even rudimentary data on the behaviour of oils in ice filled Arctic waters, no sensible contingency plan in case of accident can be developed.
That is a very serious statement made by a very serious and learned scientist. This, then, is a great challenge facing this government and facing Canada in this day and age. We cannot help but ask ourselves what the government is doing about it. We are not talking about something away off in the future; we are talking about something here and now.
We have heard from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) about his announced intention to bring in legislation known as The Northern Water Rights and Pollution Control Act. During his crusade across the country, we heard from the Minister without Portfolio about the Canada Water Act. None of us had anything but good will for the minister as he went across the country trying to prepare the people to do something about pollution. But this aspect of the problem, separated from the whole area of environmental pollution, in my view is one that requires immediate action today.

Before I resume my seat, I would like to make a few brief observations concerning the proposed legislation setting up the salt fish development corporation. Let me say to the minister and to the government that many of us in this House and in the country have waited a long time for this legislation. Indeed, we will not be satisfied until we see the legislation in the House, and perhaps even then we will not be satisfied. I know that successive governments down through the years- and here I make no exceptions-have been guilty, in my view, of grossly neglecting and ignoring the salt fish industry. As a direct consequence of this, we have seen many of our important and traditional markets lost to our European competition. As a matter of fact, one could almost suspect a conspiracy to abolish this ancient, honourable and important industry.
While the industry has been largely ignored by the federal government, the establishment has had a field day at the expense of the fishermen. Just let me illustrate what I said. Can you imagine a farmer taking his entire crop to a broker, getting from the broker an open receipt, going back to his farmhouse and waiting to see what the broker is going to pay him? He thereby places himself completely at the mercy of the broker who then sells the produce, names his own commission, and gives the farmer what is left. There is no farmer in the country who would put up with that kind of situation. Yet this ancient, feudal practice is still being carried on to this very day in the salt fish industry in Newfoundland. The tragedy of it is that our fishermen have no choice but to play along because for them there is no crop failure insurance, no government plan to advance some funds to buy gear

when they set out to catch the fish in the spring. What little they did have, such as the salt rebate program, has been taken away from them.
The salt rebate program may be peanuts to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) because we all know he is affluent, but to the fishermen of Newfoundland who are salting and drying their fish for sale it represents a great deal because their income-and statistics prove this-is barely enough to keep body and soul together. The callous treatment handed out to our fishermen-for example to those who took part in the Labrador fisheries this year and who are suffering the consequences of the failure of that fishery-has already been referred to by my colleague, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan). I have a great deal of faith in the present minister, a great deal of confidence in him, because I know he is trying to do a job. The City of St. Jean, which is the largest the county, is an industrial city where manufactures of several different descriptions are

The Address-Mr. W. Smith to be found, including chemical, carpet, cables, foundries, pottery and textiles. Many sections of Quebec have been designated as areas where manufacturers will be encouraged to build new factories. In the county of St. Jean we have some of the best market gardeners in the whole of Canada. Nevertheless, farmers in this category must be protected by limitation of imports during the summer season when their vegetables have to be marketed, principally on the Montreal market.

Since I am on the subject of Maritime Command may I say that, while I do not necessarily regret the loss of the Bonaventure, I deeply regret the loss of what it represents for ASW capacity. I believe as long as we are in the ball park we must at least bring our own glove. Maybe somebody else can supply the bats and balls, but we must at least bring our own gloves and get on the team. We must be credible. One thing that has been very clear to me in the last four years is the loss of credibility in our Maritime capability, indeed our entire defence capability, in the eyes of not only our neighbours to the south but of our partners in the North Atlantic Alliance.
In the context of Maritime Command, it is important that we do not do anything to lessen the very real expertise we have built up in the field of anti-submarine warfare. I am not talking about our capacity to destroy enemy submarines or to chase them all over the Atlantic. What I am talking about is our capacity to detect and trap submarines and to provide assistance to SACLANT, the United States and the western world. This assistance can be provided in the form of knowledge of who the underwater enemy is at any given time and where he is from day to day, once we are aware of his presence in our contiguous waters. The only way to do this is by the maintenance of a viable and credible ASW capacity.
The loss of the Bonaventure, at least to my layman's mind, represents the loss of the strongest part of one-third of the capability which we can provide to meet the very minimum standard of surveillance necessary to enable us to contribute to the total input of intelligence. Surely, in this day and age we do not need to get into the nuclear race in terms

of the capacity to kill. Surely, there is a role for us to play in detection and surveillance. I believe we can play a very meaningful role, a role that would be credible in the eyes of our partners. I believe this is very necessary. There are many ways in which we could accomplish our objective, but there is no way short of the acquisition of another aircraft carrier to replace the loss of seaborne aircraft for use in this ASW operation. Thus the loss of the Bonaventure is serious.
As one senior serving Canadian naval officer termed it, it is a bloody significant loss. I do not know that it is necessarily that, but it is certainly a very serious loss and one that we are not going to be able to readily overcome. I am not talking about the viability of our ASW operation the moment hostilities break out. I do not think we can afford to get into that type of role, but surely up to that moment, God forbid that it should ever come to pass, we can make a meaningful contribution to the total input of intelligence. I am certain that we can do our share in detection, tracking and general surveillance. There is no reason why we cannot maintain our standards. I am not asking for the world. Surely, we can maintain the minimum standards necessary to make our contribution useful.
Today's writers suggest there is a serious question about the validity of ASW operations, that there must be a meeting of minds, not so much on the technological methods involved but on the principles. We have for a long time assumed, without debate, the necessity and logic for a reasonably high contribution to this field of defence. I think there is a rationale. Most of the writings, outside the area where discussion is classified and secret, question ASW operations, but in the final analysis no suggestion is made that countries such as Canada should get out of ASW operations. Indeed, Professor Martin, a very distinguished international writer on the subject of maritime strategy suggested to the subcommittee on Maritime Command not more than two or three days ago that there is a very real need for the contribution countries like Canada can make and that it would be a shame if Canada were to let her ASW expertise spin out. The loss of the Bonaventure and the absence of a suitable replacement turn out maritime command effort in a direction in. which a spin out and run down will be a natural consequence. There is a role we can play in this area, although a limited one.

Without repeating the points he made, I should like to associate myself with his remarks and add one or two comments of my own.
I am concerned, as everyone in this House is concerned, about the effects of pollution in the north and the upsetting of the ecological balance. Canada has a responsibility to do something about this problem and it is regrettable there is not a much more intense public dialogue on the subject. It seems to me that the problem is not only a massive one but it is multinational in nature; it is not restricted to ourselves, the United States and other countries which use or plan to use the north regularly. If we look at a map of the ocean currents in the Arctic and trace those currents down to the point at which they join the waters of the Gulf Stream, we can easily imagine the consequences of a major disaster happening to a bulk carrier in our north at any time of the year. Not only would we find the waters of Hudson Bay and Labrador polluted, but the waters of the Gulf Stream itself would be affected and the mess would wind up in Europe.
It is not hard to understand the multinational consequences of a disaster in our north. If a forum were to present itself I would support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Ahuntsic (Mr. Rochon) at the NATO meetings recently for dealing with the question of the pollution of the deep seas. I would support this proposition because, to use words which were handed to me just before I rose, elocution is not the solution to pollution.
The Address-Mr. Forrestall We need to involve multinational groups in measures which are immediately effective and tangible. It seems a little ambiguous for a country like Canada to assume responsibility for pollution when it has not yet accepted legal responsibility for these waters.
It is important that we should get on with our program of providing navigational aid in the north and assistance to shipping by way of an adequate icebreaker service. As suggested by other speakers in this debate and in other forums, we ought to move rapidly in the field of research into the consequences of disasters such as an accidental oil-spill in the north. In Dartmouth in my constituency there is one of the world's leading centres for studies of the ocean. It is a matter of regret that this institute for oceanographic studies has not been directed by the government to get on with the job in the area I have mentioned.

I suggest that if the government continues in this way it will find it increasingly difficult to staff standing committees, particularly in cases where there is the slightest suspicion that the government has already made up its mind on matters referred to committees.
I could go on and talk of the waste of the taxpayers' money, but may I make just one or two references to an editorial that appeared in the Dartmouth Free Press of Thursday, September 25, 1969, and which dealt with what I consider a matter of some seriousness:
The federal government's policy of forming a number of task forces to tour the country and investigate various problems of national and international importance is a very commendable one.
I agree with that.
However, the government's reception of the reports of these groups has. to date, been somewhat amazing.
The Hon. Paul Hellyer's housing task force made a very extensive tour of the country-
I have already indicated the sort of treatment the task force received.
The Defence and External Affairs Committee toured Canada, and Canadian NATO bases in Europe, and by all indications their recommendation to maintain a strong NATO Commitment was ignored.
All members of the committee know this is true.
A subcommittee of this task force recently toured maritime command, but its recommendations were obviously not yet in the hands of the government before additional cutbacks, including HMCS Bon-aventure's disposal, were announced.

speechtext: It is a farce.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is more than a farce; it is an insult to the intelligence of the men who served on these committees.
These parliamentary groups are not touring the country with money provided from the pocket of

the Prime Minister, but with the very liberal use of taxpayers' dollars. This expenditure was justified by the committee members themselves, in most cases, for they appeared to make their investiga-tionns in a most conscientous manner. It is insulting to the members of parliament, and to the Canadian electorate who chose them for office, to have their sincere investigations apparently ignored.
These are serious times in the economic outlook of Canadians, and we can offer sympathetic understanding to some of the Liberal government's more drastic measures to reduce expenditures. However, some of the present policies indicate a contempt for Parliament and parliamentary committees which should not long be tolerated by the Canadian people.
I am surprised that the Canadian people have tolerated them even to this point. As I have indicated, this contempt for parliament is a source of embarrassment. I am sure the members of the government are conscious of this, as are the chairmen of the standing committees. In addition, a great deal of money is involved. As the editorial indicates, members of parliament seriously pursue their responsibilities in parliamentary committees. But I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you I suggest to the government, that we have a lot more to do than traipse around the countryside on futile missions while the government sits on its rear end with its mind already made up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by adopting the practice of other speakers in this debate and congratulating my colleagues, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), for their initiation of this debate on the Speech from the Throne. May I endorse the remarks made by both, but particularly those of the hon. member for Sarnia, that one is now better able to appreciate the full impact and development, the logic and planning that has gone into the program presented by the government since its election to office in June, 1968. One can see for oneself that the government is not operating on a month-to-month or on a year-to-year basis, but in fact has formulated a program that will encompass all of the power and strength that its majority position in this House enables it to do. I welcome this kind of approach to government just as much as I welcome a change that guarantees the people of this country a government that has sufficient tenure of office to enable it to plan ahead for a number of years in this fashion.
This situation can be contrasted with that of the past decade. The government of today enjoys a majority, and therefore the virtual
November 4, 1969

The Address-Mr. Jerome
certainty of a tenure of office extending over four or five years. On the other side of the coin are those less certain, hectic times when day-to-day government is imposed by a minority situation in the House-government of the sort that immediately preceded the last election. All parties in the House faced difficulties which were created by a minority government situation. It was a situation which was readily embraced by the third and fourth parties represented in the House, because truly under such circumstances can they maximize their power and position in the affairs of this chamber.
In examining the Throne Speech one readily appreciates it is a continuation and an extension of the program that was begun by the government in 1968 when the first session of this Parliament commenced. In addition to the government's attendance to the day-today needs of the country, it has had as its paramount objective during its first year of office the reform of this institution. It has changed our way of doing business so as better to enable the House to expedite its affairs in a manner more in keeping with the needs of a nation that is growing and changing so rapidly.
Having accomplished the objective of enabling this House to conduct its business more efficiently and productively, the Throne Speech that introduced the second session is, I suggest, a logical follow-up. Having reshaped our procedures here in order to enable members on all sides and of all ranks better to participate in a really meaningful study and examination of the governmental process, this administration is now turning its face inwards and is making a clear pronouncement of those domestic problems that should receive priority, and the manner in which they will be dealt with in the coming session and those to follow.
In the order in which these problems appear in the Throne Speech, they include equality, both on an economic and on a linguistic basis; our Indian population and the position of Indians; the forthcoming review of and white paper on social security, on labour and industrial relations; and also, of course, the most important problem facing Canada today, that of the inflationary trend in our economy. The Throne Speech deals with the forthcoming white paper on taxation. It deals with the problems of grain farmers. It deals with the problems of the fishing industry, water resources and Arctic sovereignty. It also deals with the position of the government
in our society. It deals with our position in respect of the Criminal law and whether one should fight to protect the liberties of the individual. It also deals with the question of consumer protection, not only in respect of credit but in respect of packaging, labelling and processing. It deals with the question of housing and outlines the prospect of one million housing starts in the forthcoming five years.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The Throne Speech deals with the government's intention to review policies in respect of external affairs, defence, citizenship, social security and taxation. Therefore, it is my pleasure to support and endorse in every way possible the Speech from the Throne which began the second session of this Parliament. As I say, it is a logical extension of the program launched in the first session of this Parliament. I support it because I know that in the forthcoming years this administration will carry on with the same logical and progressive programming which it began in 1968. I look forward to the testing of the use of the time and facilities available to the administration at the conclusion of this parliament and to a repetition of the majority mandate that we received in 1968. I look forward to such a testing at the forthcoming election, whenever it may take place.
The Speech from the Throne deals with problems that face this country at the present time. It has reference to our views on the future. Basically it places a heavy concentration of effort in the coming year on solving the problems in the areas I have mentioned. It is occupied particularly with the practical aspects of solutions to the problems we face in this country.
There are a couple of aspects of life in this country to which I should like to address myself. I believe these are important and valid considerations above and beyond the practical things of our day-to-day existence. Let me deal first with the problem of strikes. As a representative of Sudbury I perhaps speak with some reluctance on the subject of strikes. My area occupies a position of economical, educational, financial and cultural importance in northern Ontario, and it is now entering the fourth month of economic paralysis inflicted by a continuing labour dispute between the Falconbridge Nickel Company, the International Nickel Company and their
508	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Jerome respective unions-the Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers at Falconbridge and the union at INCO.
The sadness of the situation does not relate to the position in which the companies find themselves or the position in which the unions find themselves. These two companies, particularly INCO, represent the major producers of nickel and hold a virtual monopoly in the world. World markets will wait for the production of nickel, whether it be this year or next year. We have witnessed this situation in respect of Stelco. The speculators are at the present time greatly interested in and aware of the fact that at the conclusion of the strike the price of nickel will rise. The outcome will not bother them. There is nickel in the ground and these companies will eventually produce it. World speculators will obtain nickel this year or next year at a higher price. Indeed, this situation applies to a greater extent to the production of nickel than to the production of steel, because the one union involved is not as powerful as it once was in this country.
Dealing particularly with the United Steelworkers of America, that rich, strong and powerful union, let me say that it will weather this and other storms in which it is involved in Canada. In due course the members will return to work as a result of an undaunted membership. The union will perhaps increase its membership in the process. In any event, it will again begin to produce and revenues will be restored. It will become an even stronger and more powerful union through growth or amalgamation.
I am not concerned about the power struggle between the unions and the company, or which of them becomes more powerful. I am concerned about our society. We are still permitting demonstrations of hostility and war between management and labour. This seems to be the only way in which we can solve differences or disputes between these factions. The disputes involve a difference in conception of what is a fair wage. Tremendous expense is involved in this process. It is a primitive approach to arriving at a proper assessment of the value of a working man. There are differences of opinion as to how much an employee should receive in wages in order to enjoy a reasonable living.
Let me give an example of the cost of these disputes. The International Nickel dispute alone cost about 50 per cent of the total annual payroll of the city of Sudbury. That

DEBATES	November 4, 1969
strike alone cost about $42 million. The cost in terms of material that was not supplied to buyers amounted to $20 million. The loss of capital investment by the company, investment which would ordinarily have been made had the strike not taken place, amounted to about $30 million. One can add to that sum of $92 million a further sum in the neighbourhood of $120 million, representing the loss to various governments in revenue, transfer payments and taxes. This loss is obviously borne by the taxpayers.
Perhaps one could multiply that figure by two. Let us consider the fact that the International Nickel Company and the Falcon-bridge Nickel Company employ 2,300 men. This is a working force capable of sustaining a city of between 75,000 and 85,000 people for a period of four months, which is exactly the period of time these companies have not been producing. One needs very little imagination to project the effect of a strike on a community which is supported by one industry, but that is another subject. The fact is that we in this country cannot understand the position of the working man because we have been unable to develop a sense of trust between management and labour. Obviously, therefore, we cannot come to any sensible understanding of the problem or recognition of the fact that the working man should enjoy a decent standard of living.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We cannot come to a sensible recognition of the fact that a working man should enjoy an annual increment by virtue only of his seniority. We cannot recognize that a man must not be paid in year 1 the same salary one would expect him to be paid in year 10 for doing the same job. Our failure in this regard, and our leaving the entire responsibility to the give and take of economic warfare, represents a staggering expense and a crippling economic inactivity in my community. We are not alone in this regard; it is happening all over the country.
It is not easy for me to throw out on the floor of this chamber the idea that we should be able to recognize that an annual increment must be paid to every working man from time to time, and that in addition to an annual increment for seniority and longevity of service there should be a periodic adjustment based on increases in the cost of living. We know that in a period of expanding economy inflation also increases rapidly. That is not to say expansion is a bad thing. It is a
November 4, 1969
healthy thing so long as it is allowed at a controlled rate.
So we expect these fluctuations and we recognize that the working man should enjoy a share of an expanding economy. He deserves an increment and adjustment in relation to a rise in the cost of living. The plain truth of the matter is that in our country in this day and age we should be able to develop a sense of trust and responsibility between management and labour. There should not be a war between them, but there is. There should not be hostility, but there is.

speechtext: This is free enterprise.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is an aspect of free enterprise that is not working to the advantage of this country nor to the advantage of many of its participants. The man who gets the short end of the stick at every turn is the man who is punching the card and carrying the lunch-pail. Because of what he is doing to support this labour-management process, he makes a sacrifice by having to live on whatever savings he may have for as long as the fight continues. Let us take as an example the situation at Stelco. I have been told-this may be inaccurate but I believe it is close to the truth-that the difference between the offer last August and the settlement that occurred in October at Stelco in Hamilton was less than 10 cents an hour. In my opinion the price that was paid by those working people to gain another 10 cents an hour was simply not worth it. The price paid by the country was not worth it. But above all, the price paid by the working men was not worth it because they will never get back the price they paid during the life of the contract or during their lifetime.
So I say that this is one of the most important areas we must be concerned about in the future, if we are to see above and beyond the day-to-day practical necessities of this countries and our day-to-day problems. If we are to do more than simply carry out the basic functions of our job, and work for genuine progress, one of the matters to which we should be inviting the fullest attention of every member of this House is a solution to the situation I have described, namely, the primitive way in which we live, where hostility exists between the working man and his employer to the eternal detriment of the working man.
This morning I had the pleasure of listening to the remarks of the very distinguished right 21362-33
The Address-Mr. Jerome hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker). Let me hasten to say at the outset of my reference to the hon. gentleman that I hold in my hand a copy of Hansard for Tuesday, July 15 this year. The hon. gentleman is a veteran of this chamber and has achieved its highest honour, and I am a fledgling. If my seat were any farther back it would be in the lobby. He, the veteran of many sessions of parliament and one of its most experienced and able orators, holds a seat in the centre of the stronghold of Conservatism in this country. I, in beginning my career in this chamber, come from a seat in the stronghold of Liberalism in this country, northern Ontario.
I suppose our differences should be obvious because of those facts. But only this morning, when I heard the hon. gentleman devote the majority of his time in this debate to a discussion of what he described as the clandestine, and indeed subterranean plot on the part of the government to abolish the monarchy, did I realize that the difference between us could not be characterized any more clearly than was demonstrated by his major concern that there was in the Speech from the Throne an indication that the Queen does not describe this government in terms of "my government".
It is not my concern, Mr. Speaker, whether Her Majesty the Queen, whom I hold in the greatest respect, refers to this government as her government. My concern is that the young people of our country care enough about what goes on in this chamber, in this

The hon. gentleman interpreted the rule changes passed by the House last session as an attempt to adopt a system which would restrict or stifle the free exchange of ideas in this chamber. [DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I could not take a more opposite view than to say that in my view we do not have a restriction on the exchange of ideas, of intelligent opinion and of intelligent commentary, but rather a requirement that when an oratorical contribution is made to the subject under discussion speeches should be limited. This rule will force members to make intelligent, meaningful and comprehensive speeches rather than engage in a filibuster designed to do nothing more than frustrate the business of this chamber.
I was interested to hear the complaint of the hon. member for Prince Albert, that because of the intention of the government to recognize Red China we appear to be playing into the hands of those who have declared themselves avowed enemies of freedom and who remain a threat to the peaceful existence of this country and our part of the world.
Is it not a strange coincidence that the same hon. gentleman in 1961, when his administration made the first wheat sale to the U.S.S.R. to feed those people who I presume then had the same avowed intention to overthrow the free world, hailed the sale as a great achievement in the economic affairs of this country?
